items.title: Weekend hack: HackerTube. I was annoyed with YouTube's recommendations so I had Claude filter down 43M comments over 20
items.summary:
Weekend hack: HackerTube. I was annoyed with YouTube's recommendations so I had Claude filter down 43M comments over 20 years of HN to 6,454 videos that keep being recommended. *Significantly* better viewing experience, ~2 hours with Opus 5.5:
https://t.co/JIhXN7OSh1

- Excellent recs without any logins (state is kept in local browser session)
- Thumbnail is a representative frame from middle of the video instead of the super duper A/B test hyper-optimized user uploads
- Underlying data from the comment analysis as one zip file, point your Claude at it and ask for your own version
- HackerTube Longs ✊

A bit more on the process:
I use Claude Code (desktop app for Mac), Opus 5.5 on Medium effort as my default. I only talk to Claude and have it do everything, the only "manual work" I helped with in tandem was in the browser (reminiscent of MenuGen): 1) I had to create some kind of API key from Google Cloud UI to query YouTube for video metadata, 2) I booted up a VPS box for serving and 3) I bought the domain name. Once the box was up I gave Claude the IP and told it update, secure, harden, deploy and optimize the code, and it did the whole thing.

Many awesome projects that would have normally taken weeks/months even can now be few-shotted for breakfast. What else are we not thinking of.

items.title: Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now les
items.summary:
Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now less "two groups of people speaking past each other" and more a sharp funnel.

- Napkin math somewhere around 6B people (~75% of the population) have barely come in contact with LLMs at all.
- Around 1-2B (~20%) are casual and infrequent users of free-tier ChatGPT-like products. This group sees derpy chatbots and treats them a bit like a better Google search, a writing aid, or etc. Maybe an agent tries to book you a flight. I have non-tech friends who (reasonably, imo) say they have not much use for it at all. Even many professionals outside of math&code are in this tier. For example, execs and many other functions spend a lot of their time talking to other people, so while they understand what is happening intellectually, it is still second-hand and a bit abstract.
- Now we get to professional use of frontier-grade LLMs in math&code. Somewhere around 20M people (0.2%) see first-hand that large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt. Building apps, copying apps, translating apps, decompiling apps from binaries... This has all happened very quickly and recently - less than 1 year ago, I was writing code manually by hand, typing memorized computer code commands into a code editor character by character, occasionally pressing Tab to autocomplete a little chunk of code.
- And finally we get to the ~5,000 people (~0.00006%) with access to frontier-grade systems internally. The external world has seen the preview. It looks like swarms of thousands of agents collaborating over weeks on software mega projects: minting zero days, running cyber attacks and defenses at machine speeds, discovering new science, advancing the frontier of mathematics. Things that would have taken top professionals in the industry years of work. Meanwhile, human review and comprehension are starting to fall behind. For example, people are still involved in the "archeology" of the OpenAI-HF incident from many months ago. Mathematicians may be poring over the 722 manuscripts on frontier mathematics for a while.

The funnel is driven by a combination of factors:
1. The impact scales with ambition, problem size, and horizon. A question with a paragraph answer barely stresses the system. You need a reservoir of big, difficult problems that you really care about. This aspect drives the consumer / professional dimension of the funnel.
2. The jaggedness of the system (which I have written about a lot separately). Capability peaks in domains that are digital, verifiable and economically valuable. This is because LLM capability emerges from reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards on a curated environment mixture driven by revenue potential. This aspect primarily drives the area (e.g. math&code) dimension of the funnel.
3. Access. Free-tier, paid-tier, internal.

So this is the weirdness of the moment. The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems. When they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot. The majority of professionals still see only a modest uplift. And a small sliver of professionals are experiencing the vertigo of the curve going vertical. And it is all happening at the same time.

items.title: We'll be spending a lot more time trying to understand the outputs of language models. A few thoughts, tips & tricks:
items.summary:
We'll be spending a lot more time trying to understand the outputs of language models. A few thoughts, tips & tricks:

Writing. Something I've had success with: Ask your LLM to explain something in ASD-STE100, it's a controlled language specification originally developed for aerospace maintenance documentation. LLMs well-versed in this language and it comes with heavy constraints on clean writing style that I often find a lot more readable. Sometimes I've tried to soften it a bit e.g. ask for "80% of the way to ASD-STE100" because the spec is quite stringent. But even better:

Diagrams / images. Instead of writing, ask your LLM to create a diagram. These can be a lot easier to process, parse, and understand. But even better:

Web pages. Ask for output "in HTML" to get a beautiful, interactive webpage. LLMs are getting really good at frontend and can create beautiful experiences, animations, etc. But even better:

Explainer videos. The output format I am most bullish on is fully custom / bespoke explainer videos generated on any arbitrary topic. Experiment with things like "Create a 3b1b style video explainer on X. Use my ElevenLabs API key for audio narration". (you'd need an API key for the latter or you can ask your LLM to find you decent free alternatives that use your local compute). This is actually starting to work!

In summary:
- As LLMs get better, they will do more and more of the legwork autonomously, and a lot more of our work will rise up the abstractions into oversight and understanding.
- Luckily, LLMs can help here too because as intelligence and code are increasingly abundant, you can ask for large, custom, discardable software artifacts (e.g. web apps, video explainers) that would have never made sense to create before. Push the boundaries here and you'll be surprised.

items.title: AI Field Notes #134
items.summary:
AI Field Notes #134

Gemini 4 Carbon is public at $2 per million input tokens, and the price doubles on December 1. It also burns more tokens per task than the model it sits above.

- Artificial Analysis: $7.76 per solved task vs $6.25 for GPT-6 Astra Max
- Claude now runs Adobe and Atlassian apps inside the chat on the open MCP Apps spec
- An official MCP demo server leaked API keys to any open browser tab; fixed in 2.0.1
- Co-Design Bench: the best coding agent fully finishes 26.4% of real change requests

TODAY'S STORIES:

1. Gemini 4 Carbon goes public at $2 per million tokens, and the price doubles December 1
Backend engineers picking a model for hard debugging should price it per finished task, with December's rate plugged in. Run ten of your ugliest tickets through Carbon this month while it is cheap. GitHub Copilot added it the same day, so the test costs you an afternoon.

2. Claude interactive connectors: Adobe, Atlassian and HubSpot apps now run inside the chat
Frontend developers at a software company just got a new surface to build for. It is an open spec, so the work should carry beyond Claude. Start with one workflow your customers already ask a chatbot about, and remember that admins can still restrict which connector tools are allowed.

3. MCP reference server leaked API keys to any web page a developer had open
Upgrade server-everything to 2.0.1 and rotate every key that sat in its environment. The SDK fix in 2.3.0 refuses shared instances, so an engineer running an HTTP MCP server should expect a small rewrite. For FastMCP, version 4.1.2 is half the job: you also have to set the new issuer parameter.

4. Co-Design Bench: the best coding agent fully finishes 26.4% of real change requests
A tech lead budgeting for agents should plan on a human finishing nearly three of every four tickets. Ask vendors which harness their scores came from, because the same model ranked differently in different ones. Small edits from a receipt or a screenshot went best, and whole-repository changes went worst.

5. Claude Fable 5.2 designed three circuit boards that worked without a single wiring fix
Hardware engineers who lay out boards for a living just watched the first-draft part of the job done by a model. Validation, certification and manufacturing at volume still need you. Anthropic has a commercial relationship with Diode, so read this as a vendor's report that happens to come with working hardware.

6. Claude Meetings joins Google Meet calls and drafts the plan while people talk
Project managers and chiefs of staff, the people who turn a meeting into a task list, will see that step done before the call ends. What is left is deciding which of the drafted tasks are wrong. Look at the admin setting for external guests before your next client call.

7. Businesses in ChatGPT: OpenAI gives brands verified profiles and their own sales agents
A marketing manager at an online shop has a new storefront to staff, and it talks. Claim the profile and fix your prices before a customer asks the agent. If you pay a tool to estimate your ChatGPT visibility, compare its numbers with OpenAI's own dashboard.

8. Mercor doubles to a $20B valuation on 5 million experts training AI models
Lawyers, doctors and accountants picking up evaluation gigs are selling the judgment that makes the next model better at their job. The pay is real today. Ask what data the platform keeps about you, since the April breach went unmentioned in the celebration.

9. Nvidia hires ex-prosecutor Joon Kim to investigate Jensen Huang as shareholders sue
Nothing changes this month for a machine learning engineer waiting on GPUs. The exposure is political: the probe touches what Nvidia knew about restricted chips reaching China, and that could tighten export rules. Teams with a single-vendor hardware plan have six weeks to think about a second one.

10. SoftBank books a $3.7B loss on power gear it ordered early for US AI data centers
The scramble for turbines and transformers has reached the stage where early orders become write-offs. A utility engineer or facilities planner should treat announced gigawatts as plans that can change. For everyone else, this is one more sign the buildout's bills arrive before its revenue.

11. Stanford AI100 report: scaling is running out of road and AI is 'not yet paying its way'
Students choosing what to study should note where the panel expects progress: algorithms and efficiency, areas a small team can work on. A manager asked to prove AI savings is in good company, since the economy-wide numbers are not there yet either.

ONE STORY THAT MOVES THE FLOOR:

The PCB layout engineer opening a blank board this week has a new rival. Claude Fable 5.2 designed three devices with Diode Computers, wrote its own router in about half an hour, and all three prototypes worked with no circuitry fixes. Its layout score went from 25% on Fable 5 to 69%. Which hardware task on your bench still needs a person for the first draft?

Full issue with sources, plus the daily email: link in my profile.

items.title: Qwen3.8-27B Turbo has reportedly passed 1.37 million downloads on Hugging Face, with an 11.67GB checkpoint and an advert
items.summary:
Qwen3.8-27B Turbo has reportedly passed 1.37 million downloads on Hugging Face, with an 11.67GB checkpoint and an advertised 256K-token context window.

It combines four things that make it interesting for local AI development: a relatively compact 27B model, Apache 2.0 licensing, a large context window and creator-reported low refusal rates.

But the specifications deserve a closer look.

1. A 27B model in an 11.67GB checkpoint

An 11.67GB download makes the model easier to store and experiment with than many larger checkpoints.

For developers building local coding agents, that lowers the initial barrier to testing a model of this size.

There is an important distinction, though: checkpoint size is not the same as total inference memory.

Running the model also requires memory for:

KV cache: Stores information from previously processed tokens.
Activations: Holds intermediate values generated during computation.
Runtime buffers: Provides memory for internal inference operations.

These requirements change with context length, batch size, quantisation and the inference engine.

So, an 11.67GB checkpoint does not automatically mean the model will run comfortably on a 12GB GPU. The weights are only part of the memory requirement.

2. Apache 2.0 gives developers more flexibility

The Apache 2.0 licence is another important part of the release.

Subject to its terms, developers can use the model commercially, modify it, redistribute it and integrate it into their own applications.

That opens up several possibilities:

Building local AI coding tools.
Integrating the model into autonomous agent systems.
Creating custom inference pipelines.
Fine-tuning and distributing modified versions.

Developers aren’t limited to accessing the model through a proprietary API. They have more control over how they deploy and adapt it.

3. The uncensored claim needs independent testing

The creator presents Qwen3.8-27B Turbo as an uncensored coding model and reports zero refusals across 100 test prompts.

For technical workflows, fewer unnecessary refusals could be useful. Debugging, security research, code analysis and other specialised tasks can sometimes be interrupted by overly restrictive model behaviour.

However, answering more prompts does not automatically mean producing better answers.

Refusal rates tell us something about a model’s behaviour, not whether it can solve difficult coding problems, follow complex instructions or generate reliable code.

The reported 0/100 result also reflects the creator’s selected prompts. It isn’t proof that the model will never refuse a request.

Independent evaluations would help establish how consistently it behaves across different tasks.

4. The 256K context window could help with repository-level coding

A coding agent needs more than the contents of one source file.

It may have to inspect an entire repository, understand dependencies, read documentation, examine configuration files, track previous changes and process tool outputs before deciding what to do next.

An advertised 256K-token context window gives the model more room to handle that information within a single interaction.

But there is a hardware trade-off.

As more tokens enter the context, the KV cache grows, increasing VRAM or system RAM consumption. Generation speed can also decline as the context gets longer.

Supporting 256K tokens doesn’t mean every consumer GPU can run that context efficiently.

Reported specifications

Model: Qwen3.8-27B Turbo
Parameters: 27B
Checkpoint size: 11.67GB
Licence: Apache 2.0
Context window: 256K tokens
Refusal evaluation: 0/100 prompts, creator-reported
Hugging Face downloads: 1.37 million reported
Access: Reported as free, with no access restrictions

What still needs to be tested?

The specifications make this release worth investigating, but download numbers and refusal tests don’t establish how capable it is as a coding model.

I’d particularly like to see independent results covering:

items.title: IBM đưa máy tính lượng tử Quantum System Two vào hoạt động tại Chicago
items.summary:
Một số hướng nghiên cứu đã được triển khai. Deloitte và AbbVie đang phối hợp với IBM và Đại học Northwestern nghiên cứu mô phỏng phn tử lượng tử phục vụ phát triển thuốc. Trong lĩnh vực năng lượng, EPRI cùng Đại học Illinois Urbana-Champaign tìm hiểu khả năng ứng dụng thuật toán tối ưu lượng tử nhằm nng cao hiệu quả vận hành lưới điện. [...] Về lu dài, Quantum System Two sẽ chuyển đến IQMP sau khi khu công nghệ này hoàn thành xy dựng. Hiện hệ thống vẫn hoạt động tại Hyde Park Labs, chưa chuyển sang địa điểm mới.

Việc đưa thiết bị vào vận hành tạo thêm điều kiện phát triển hạ tầng nghiên cứu lượng tử dùng chung. Tuy nhiên, những ứng dụng trong dược phẩm và năng lượng hiện chủ yếu ở giai đoạn nghiên cứu; các công bố chưa cung cấp số liệu độc lập chứng minh hiệu quả thương mại từ hệ thống mới. [...] Thông qua trung tm này, các trường đại học, phòng thí nghiệm quốc gia, doanh nghiệp và startup có thể hợp tác với các nhà nghiên cứu IBM để phát triển thuật toán, tìm kiếm ứng dụng điện toán lượng tử trong thực tế.

items.title: Operation-aware Multimodal Clinical Decision Support System for ICU Discharge Risk Assessment
items.summary: Unplanned 30-day intensive care unit (ICU) readmission is a critical benchmark for evaluating healthcare quality. Most predictive models assume readmission risk depends solely on a patient's individual pathophysiological state, ignoring hospital operational context and resource capacity. In practice, discharge decisions are dynamic trade-offs between patient stability and bed turnover pressures. To address this gap, we develop an Operation-aware Multimodal Clinical Decision Support System (CDSS) for ICU discharge risk assessment. The system combines multi-agent collaborative extraction with self-evolving retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to eliminate template noise from progress notes, while constructing departmental workload indicators alongside admission flow features, continuous vital signs, and sparse medical codes (ICD/DRG). Addressing severe class imbalance (about 10.5% readmissions) and alarm fatigue, we implement data normalization, class reweighting, and decision-threshold calibration. In 20 independent runs across 20,000 ICU stays from MIMIC-III, empirical findings demonstrate that: vital signs alone have limited predictive capacity under real-world class imbalance (PR-AUC of 0.1387 +/- 0.0086); directly concatenating raw text embeddings degrades decision tree performance (XGBoost and LightGBM PR-AUC drop to 0.3893 and 0.4030); whereas an end-to-end multimodal fine-tuning architecture (Transformer E2E FineTune) utilizing layer-wise parameter freezing and differential learning rates reverses text negative transfer, achieving the highest AUROC of 0.8288 +/- 0.0110, PR-AUC of 0.4373 +/- 0.0310, and F1-Score of 0.4757 +/- 0.0196. Operational indicators supply independent risk signals, laying an engineering foundation for high-utility clinical decision support tools.

items.title: MMGraph-Agent: Agentic Multimodal RAG via Cache-Inspired Multimodal Knowledge HyperGraphs
items.summary: Driven by increasingly complex real-world applications, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has evolved from textual pipelines to multimodal settings, comprising two complementary dimensions: knowledge organization and retrieval enhancement. However, existing methods still face challenges of high construction cost, context window limitations, and the lack of unified training across offline and online knowledge sources. To address these challenges, we propose MMGraph-Agent, a unified multimodal RAG framework based on cache-inspired multimodal knowledge hypergraphs. MMGraph-Agent enables extremely lightweight hypergraph construction with zero API cost and dynamic memory-based retrieval that alleviates long-context issues. Experiments across offline, online, and joint retrieval settings demonstrate consistent improvements in performance, efficiency, and architectural unification. Our software and data are publicly available at https://github.com/LHRLAB/MMGraph-Agent.

items.title: Fundus-R1: Training a Fundus-Reading MLLM on Public Data
items.summary: Fundus imaging such as CFP, OCT and SLO is crucial for the early detection of retinal anomalies and diseases. Fundus image understanding, due to its knowledge-intensive nature, poses a challenging vision-language task. An emerging approach to addressing the task is to post-train a generic multimodal large language model (MLLM), either by supervised finetuning (SFT) or by reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), on a considerable amount of in-house samples paired with high-quality clinical reports. However, these valuable samples are not publicly accessible, which not only hinders reproducibility but also practically limits research to few players. In this paper, we make a novel attempt to train a reasoning-enhanced fundus-reading MLLM, termed Fundus-R1, using exclusively public datasets, wherein over 94% of the data are annotated with image-level labels only. Our technical contributions are two-fold. First, we propose a RAG-based method for composing image-specific, knowledge-aware reasoning traces. Such auto-generated traces link visual findings identified by a generic MLLM to the image labels in terms of ophthalmic knowledge. Second, we enhance RLVR with a process reward that encourages self-consistency of the generated reasoning trace in each rollout. Extensive experiments on three fundus-reading benchmarks, i.e., FunBench, Omni-Fundus and GMAI-Fundus, show that Fundus-R1 clearly outperforms multiple baselines, including its generic counterpart (Qwen2.5-VL) and a stronger edition post-trained without using the generated traces. This work paves the way for training powerful fundus-reading MLLMs with publicly available data.

items.title: arXiv paper 2401.12345
items.summary:
arXiv:2401.12345v3  [eess.SP]  17 Jun 2025
1
Distributionally Robust Receive Combining
Shixiong Wang, Wei Dai, and Geoffrey Ye Li, Fellow, IEEE
Abstract—This article investigates signal estimation in wireless
transmission (i.e., receive combining) from the perspective of
statistical machine learning, where the transmit signals may be
from an integrated sensing and communication system; that is,
1) signals may be not only discrete constellation points but also
arbitrary complex values; 2) signals may be spatially correlated.
Particular attention is paid to handling various uncertainties
such as the uncertainty of the transmit signal covariance, the
uncertainty of the channel matrix, the uncertainty of the channel
noise covariance, the existence of channel impulse noises, the non-
ideality of the power amplifiers, and the limited sample size of
pilots. To proceed, a distributionally robust receive combining
framework that is insensitive to the above uncertainties is
proposed, which reveals that channel estimation is not a necessary
operation. For optimal linear estimation, the proposed framework
includes several existing combiners as special cases such as diag-
onal loading and eigenvalue thresholding. For optimal nonlinear
estimation, estimators are limited in reproducing kernel Hilbert
spaces and neural network function spaces, and corresponding
uncertainty-aware solutions (e.g., kernelized diagonal loading)
are derived. In addition, we prove that the ridge and kernel
ridge regression methods in machine learning are distributionally
robust against diagonal perturbation in feature covariance.
Index Terms —Wireless Transmission, Smart Antenna, Ma-
chine Learning, Robust Estimation, Robust Combining, Distri-
butional Uncertainty, Channel Uncertainty, Limited Pilot.
I. I NTRODUCTION
I
N wireless transmission, detection and estimation of trans-
mitted signals is of high importance, and combining at
array receivers serves as a key signal-processing technique to
suppress interference and environmental noises. The earliest
beamforming solutions rely on the use of phase shifters (e.g.,
phased arrays) to steer and shape wave lobes, while advanced
combining methods allow the employment of digital signal
processing units, which introduce additional structural freedom
(e.g., fully digital, hybrid, nonlinear, wideband) in combiner
design and significant performance improvement in signal
recovery [1]–[3].
In traditional communication systems, transmitted signals
are discrete points from constellations. Therefore, signal re-
covery, commonly referred to as signal detection, can be cast
into a classification problem from the perspective of statistical
machine learning, and the number of candidate classes is
determined by the number of points in the employed constel-
lation. Research in this stream includes, e.g., [4]–[9] as well
as references therein, and the performance measure for signal
detection is usually the misclassification rate (i.e., symbol error

and Electronic Engineering, Imperial College London, London SW7 2AZ,
United Kingdom (E-mail: s.wang@u.nus.edu; wei.dai1@imperial.ac.uk; ge-
offrey.li@imperial.ac.uk).
This work is supported by the UK Department for Science, Innovation
and Technology under the Future Open Networks Research Challenge project
TUDOR (Towards Ubiquitous 3D Open Resilient Network).
rate); representative algorithms encompass the maximum like-
lihood detector, the sphere decoding, etc. In another research
stream, the signal recovery performance is evaluated using
mean-squared errors (cf., signal-to-interference-plus-noise ra-
tio), and the resultant signal recovery problem is commonly
known as signal estimation , which can be considered as a
regression problem from the perspective of statistical machine
learning. By comparing the estimated symbols with the con-
stellation points afterward, the detection of discrete symbols
can be realized. For this case, till now, typical combining solu-
tions include zero-forcing receivers, Wiener receivers (i.e., lin-
ear minimum mean-squared error receivers), Capon receivers
(i.e., minimum variance distortionless response receivers), and
nonlinear receivers such as neural-network receivers [10]–[12].
On the basis of these canonical approaches, variants such
as robust beamformers working against the limited size of
pilot samples and the uncertainty in steering vectors [13]–
[18] have also been intensively reported; among these robust
solutions, the diagonal loading method [19], [14, Eq. (11)]
and the eigenvalue thresholding method [20], [14, Eq. (12)]
are popular due to their excellent balance between practical
performance and technical simplicity.
Different from traditional paradigms, in emerging commu-
nication systems, e.g., integrated sensing and communication
(ISAC) systems, transmitted signals may be arbitrary complex
values and spatially correlated [21]–[23]. As a result, mean-
squared error is a preferred performance measure to investigate
the receive combining and estimation problem of wireless
signals, which is, therefore, the focus of this article.
Although a large body of problems have been attacked in the
area, the following signal-processing problems of combining
and estimation in wireless transmission remain unsolved.
1) What is the relation between the signal-model-based
approaches (e.g., Wiener and Capon receivers) and the
data-driven approaches (e.g., deep-learning receivers)? In
other words, how can we build a mathematically unified
modeling framework to interpret all the existing digital
receive combiners?
2) In addition to the limited pilot size and the uncertainty
in steering vectors, there exist other uncertainties in
the signal model: the uncertainty of the transmit signal
covariance, the uncertainty of the communication channel
matrix, the uncertainty of the channel noise covariance,
the presence of channel impulse noises (i.e., outliers), and
the non-ideality of the power amplifiers. Therefore, how
can we handle all these types of uncertainties in a unified
solution framework?
3) Existing literature mainly studied the robustness theory
of linear beamformers against limited pilot size and the
uncertainty in steering vectors [13]–[18]. However, how
can we develop the theory of robust nonlinear combiners

2
against all the aforementioned uncertainties?
To this end, this article designs a unified modeling and
solution framework for receive combining of wireless signals,
in consideration of the scarcity of the pilot data and the
different uncertainties in the signal model.
A. Contributions
The contributions of this article can be summarized from the
aspects of machine learning theory and wireless transmission
theory.
In terms of machine learning theory, we give a justification
of the popular ridge regression and kernel ridge regression
(i.e., quadratic loss function plus squared- F -norm regulariza-
tion) from the perspective of distributional robustness against
diagonal perturbation in feature covariance, which enriches the
theory of trustworthy machine learning; see Theorems 2 and
3, as well as Corollaries 3 and 5.
In terms of wireless transmission theory, the contributions
are outlined below.
1) We build a fundamentally theoretical framework for re-
ceive combining from the perspective of statistical ma-
chine learning. In addition to the linear estimation meth-
ods, nonlinear approaches (i.e., nonlinear combining) are
also discussed in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces and
neural network function spaces. In particular, we reveal
that channel estimation is not a necessary operation in
receive combining. For details, see Subsection III-A.
2) The presented framework is particularly developed from
the perspective of distributional robustness which can
therefore combat the limited size of pilot data and several
types of uncertainties in the wireless signal model such
as the uncertainty in the transmit power matrix, the
